reminder: Convolving with ever narrower bumps of integral one gives functions that converge to the original function.
definition: An approximation of the identity is a family $(\varphi_\varepsilon)_{\varepsilon>0}$ of functions on $\mathbb{R}^n$ with $\varphi_\varepsilon\ge0$ and $\int\varphi_\varepsilon=1$, such that the mass of $\varphi_\varepsilon$ outside every fixed ball around $0$ tends to $0$ as $\varepsilon\to0$. For a continuous function $f$ with compact support, the [convolution](c:convolution) $f*\varphi_\varepsilon$ then tends to $f$ uniformly, so the family acts like the missing identity of convolution, the [Dirac distribution](c:dirac-distribution). This is the standard way to show that nice functions are [dense](c:dense-set) in a function space.
examples: Take a smooth bump $\varphi\ge0$ with integral $1$ and set $\varphi_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$.
The heat kernels $(4\pi t)^{-n/2}e^{-|x|^2/4t}$ form an approximation of the identity as $t\to0$.
The Fejér kernels on the circle form an approximation of the identity for Fourier series.
Non-example: the Dirichlet kernels $D_N$ are not an approximation of the identity, because they take negative values and $\int|D_N|\to\infty$.

steps: Take a smooth function $\varphi\ge0$ with compact support and $\int\varphi=1$.
Set $\varphi_\varepsilon(x)=\varepsilon^{-n}\varphi(x/\varepsilon)$, which keeps the integral equal to $1$.
If the support of $\varphi$ lies in a ball of radius $R$, then $\varphi_\varepsilon$ vanishes outside the ball of radius $\varepsilon R$.
So the mass of $\varphi_\varepsilon$ outside any fixed ball is $0$ for small $\varepsilon$, and the [mollifier](c:mollifier) family is an approximation of the identity.
links.why: It shows that mollifiers are the smooth, compactly supported case, so they inherit the convergence of $f*\varphi_\varepsilon$ to $f$.

reminder: For every positive $y$ and every $x$, some natural multiple of $y$ is at least $x$.
definition: An [ordered additive monoid](c:is-ordered-add-monoid) $M$ is Archimedean when for all $x,y\in M$ with $0<y$ there is a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ with $x\le n\cdot y$, where $n\cdot y$ is the sum of $n$ copies of $y$. So no positive element is infinitely small compared with another.
examples: $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ with the usual order are Archimedean: for $0<y$ any integer $n>x/y$ works.
Every additive subgroup of $\mathbb{R}$, such as $\mathbb{Z}$, is Archimedean, because it inherits the order of $\mathbb{R}$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}$ with the lexicographic order is not Archimedean, because $n\cdot(0,1)<(1,0)$ for every $n$.
Non-example: the ordered field $\mathbb{R}(x)$ in which $x$ is larger than every real number is not Archimedean.

steps: Let $F$ be an [ordered field](c:ordered-field).
The addition of $F$ makes $(F,+,\le)$ an ordered additive monoid.
Call $F$ Archimedean when this monoid is Archimedean.
Then $F$ is an [Archimedean ordered field](c:archimedean-ordered-field).
links.why: It shows that the Archimedean property of a field is the monoid property applied to its addition.

reminder: Two elements of an ordered abelian group lie in one class when each is bounded by a multiple of the other.
definition: Let $G$ be an [ordered abelian group](c:ordered-abelian-group) with a total order, and let $|x|$ be the larger of $x$ and $-x$. Two elements $x,y$ are Archimedean equivalent when $|x|\le n|y|$ and $|y|\le n|x|$ for some [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$. This is an [equivalence relation](c:equivalence-relation), and its classes are the Archimedean classes, ordered by $[x]<[y]$ when $n|x|<|y|$ for every $n$.
examples: In $\mathbb{R}$ there are only two classes: $\{0\}$ and the set of all nonzero reals.
In $\mathbb{Z}^2$ with the lexicographic order there are three classes: $\{0\}$, the elements $(0,b)$ with $b\ne0$, and the elements $(a,b)$ with $a\ne0$.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{Z}^2$ with the lexicographic order, $(0,1)$ and $(1,0)$ lie in different classes, because $n\cdot(0,1)<(1,0)$ for all $n$.

reminder: The arithmetical hierarchy sorts sets of natural numbers by how many alternating quantifiers their defining formulas need.
definition: Call a relation on $\mathbb{N}$ $\Sigma^0_0$, $\Pi^0_0$ and $\Delta^0_0$ when a [first-order](c:first-order-logic) formula of arithmetic with only bounded quantifiers defines it. For $n\ge1$, a set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is $\Sigma^0_n$ when $x\in A\iff\exists y\,B(x,y)$ for some $\Pi^0_{n-1}$ relation $B$; it is $\Pi^0_n$ when its complement is $\Sigma^0_n$, and $\Delta^0_n$ when it is both. Every class contains the classes of lower levels, so the classes form a hierarchy of sets of [natural numbers](c:natural-number).
examples: The $\Delta^0_1$ sets are the [computable sets](c:computable-set), and the $\Sigma^0_1$ sets are the computably enumerable sets, such as the halting set.
The set of codes of Turing machines that halt on every input is $\Pi^0_2$, because it is defined by $\forall x\,\exists s$ (the machine halts on $x$ within $s$ steps).
Non-example: the halting set is not $\Pi^0_1$, because then both it and its complement would be computably enumerable, and the halting set would be computable.

reminder: The associator of three elements is $(xy)z-x(yz)$, which is zero exactly when the product is associative on them.
definition: In a [nonassociative algebra](c:nonassociative-algebra) $A$, the associator is the map $A\times A\times A\to A$ given by $(x,y,z)=(xy)z-x(yz)$. It is trilinear, so it is a [multilinear map](c:multilinear-map), and $A$ is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) exactly when the associator is zero.
examples: In $(\mathbb{R}^3,\times)$ the associator is not zero: $(e_1,e_1,e_2)=(e_1\times e_1)\times e_2-e_1\times(e_1\times e_2)=e_2$.
In an associative algebra such as the matrix algebra $M_n(\mathbb{R})$ the associator is zero for all arguments.

In a [monoidal category](c:monoidal-category) the associativity isomorphism $(X\otimes Y)\otimes Z\to X\otimes(Y\otimes Z)$ is also called the associator; it replaces the equation $(xy)z=x(yz)$ by a natural isomorphism.
Non-example: the commutator $xy-yx$ is not the associator, because it has two arguments and measures failure of commutativity.

reminder: A morphism attaches cells $g_a$ when its target is the pushout of a coproduct of the $g_a$ along a map into its source.
definition: Let $g_a:A_a\to B_a$ be a family of morphisms of a [category](c:category), and let $f:X_1\to X_2$ be a morphism. Then $f$ attaches cells of the form $g_a$ when there is a map $\coprod_aA_a\to X_1$ such that $X_2$ is the [pushout](c:pushout) of $\coprod_ag_a:\coprod_aA_a\to\coprod_aB_a$ along it, and $f$ is the induced map from $X_1$, where the [coproducts](c:coproduct) are taken in the category.
examples: In topological spaces take $g:S^{n-1}\to D^n$: gluing one $2$-cell to a point along the constant map $S^1\to\mathrm{pt}$ gives $S^2$.
A [CW complex](c:cw-complex) is built from the empty space by attaching cells, one dimension after another.
With an empty family of cells the pushout adds nothing, so every identity morphism attaches cells.
Non-example: the map $\mathrm{pt}\to\mathrm{pt}\sqcup\mathrm{pt}$ does not attach cells $S^{n-1}\to D^n$ with $n\ge1$, because such an attachment keeps a connected space connected.

reminder: An attractor is a compact invariant set that all nearby orbits approach as time goes on.
definition: Let $\varphi_t$ be the flow of a [dynamical system](c:dynamical-system) on a space $X$. A set $A\subseteq X$ is an attractor when it is [compact](c:compact-space) and invariant ($\varphi_t(A)=A$ for all $t$), and it has an open neighbourhood $U$ such that $\operatorname{dist}(\varphi_t(x),A)\to0$ as $t\to\infty$ for every $x\in U$. Many authors also require that $A$ cannot be split into two smaller attractors.
examples: For $\dot x=-x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ the [fixed point](c:fixed-point) $0$ is an attractor, and it attracts every orbit.
For $\dot r=r(1-r^2)$, $\dot\theta=1$ the circle $r=1$ is an attractor (a stable limit cycle), and it attracts every orbit except the origin.
The Lorenz system has a strange attractor, a compact invariant set with fractal structure.
Non-example: for $\dot x=x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ the point $0$ is invariant but not an attractor, because nearby orbits move away from it.

reminder: An augmented algebra has an algebra map $\varepsilon:A\to R$ that sends each scalar $r\cdot1$ to $r$.
definition: Let $R$ be a [commutative ring](c:commutative-ring). An augmented $R$-algebra is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) $A$ over $R$ together with an $R$-algebra [homomorphism](c:homomorphism) $\varepsilon:A\to R$, the augmentation, so that $\varepsilon(r\cdot1_A)=r$ for every $r\in R$. The [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) of $\varepsilon$ is the [augmentation ideal](c:augmentation-ideal), and $A=R\cdot1\oplus\ker\varepsilon$.
examples: The [group algebra](c:group-algebra) $R[G]$ has the augmentation $\varepsilon(\sum a_gg)=\sum a_g$.
The [polynomial ring](c:polynomial-ring) $R[x]$ has the augmentation $\varepsilon(p)=p(0)$, the evaluation at $0$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{C}$ as an $\mathbb{R}$-algebra has no augmentation, because a homomorphism $\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{R}$ would send $i$ to a real number whose square is $-1$.

steps: Start with an augmented algebra $(A,\varepsilon)$ over $R$.
Forget the map $\varepsilon$ and keep the ring $A$ with its map $R\to A$.
What remains is an [associative algebra](c:associative-algebra) over $R$.
The augmented case adds one more map $\varepsilon:A\to R$ with $\varepsilon(r\cdot1)=r$.
links.why: It shows that an augmentation is extra structure on an algebra, not a new kind of algebra.

reminder: The augmented matrix of a linear system $Ax=b$ is the matrix $A$ with the column $b$ added on the right.
definition: For a [system of linear equations](c:system-of-linear-equations) $Ax=b$ over a field, with coefficient [matrix](c:matrix) $A$ of size $m\times n$ and right-hand side $b$, the augmented matrix is the $m\times(n+1)$ matrix $[A\mid b]$ whose last column is $b$. Row operations on $[A\mid b]$ match operations on the equations that keep the solution set. The system has a solution exactly when the [rank](c:rank-of-a-matrix) of $A$ equals the rank of $[A\mid b]$ (the Rouché–Capelli theorem).
examples: The system $x+2y=3$, $4x+5y=6$ has the augmented matrix $\left(\begin{array}{cc|c}1&2&3\\4&5&6\end{array}\right)$.
The system $x+y=1$, $x+y=2$ has $A$ of rank $1$ but $[A\mid b]$ of rank $2$, so it has no solution.
Non-example: the coefficient matrix $A$ alone is not the augmented matrix, because it forgets the right-hand side $b$.

reminder: The axiom of infinity says that some set contains the empty set and, with each member $x$, also $x\cup\{x\}$.
definition: In [ZF set theory](c:zf-set-theory), the axiom of infinity says that an inductive [set](c:set) exists: a set $I$ with $\varnothing\in I$ such that $x\in I$ implies that the [successor](c:successor) $x\cup\{x\}$ is in $I$. Such a set is [infinite](c:infinite-set), and the smallest inductive set is the set $\omega$ of [natural numbers](c:natural-number). The other axioms of ZF do not prove that an infinite set exists.
examples: The set $\omega=\{0,1,2,\dots\}$ with $0=\varnothing$ and $n+1=n\cup\{n\}$ is the smallest inductive set.
With the axiom, the sets $\mathbb{N}$, $\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{R}$ can be built, because the other axioms construct them from $\omega$.
Non-example: no finite set is inductive, because the sets $\varnothing,\{\varnothing\},\{\varnothing,\{\varnothing\}\},\dots$ are all different.

reminder: An axiom schema is one template that gives a separate axiom for each formula that fills its placeholder.
definition: An axiom schema is a [formula](c:formula) template with a placeholder, which is a formula variable or a parameter. It stands for the infinite family of [axioms](c:axiom) that come from replacing the placeholder by each formula of the language, so a [deductive system](c:deductive-system) with a schema has one axiom for each instance.
examples: The separation schema of ZF: for each formula $\varphi(x)$ and each set $A$, the set $\{x\in A:\varphi(x)\}$ exists.
The induction schema of [Peano arithmetic](c:peano-arithmetic): for each formula $\varphi(n)$, if $\varphi(0)$ and $\forall n\,(\varphi(n)\to\varphi(n+1))$ hold, then $\forall n\,\varphi(n)$.
Non-example: the axiom of extensionality is one sentence without a placeholder, so it is a single axiom and not a schema.

reminder: Extend finite partial isomorphisms alternately on each side to build an isomorphism of two countable structures.
definition: Let $A$ and $B$ be [countable](c:countable-set) structures with elements listed as $a_0,a_1,\dots$ and $b_0,b_1,\dots$. The back-and-forth method builds finite partial [isomorphisms](c:isomorphism) $p_0\subseteq p_1\subseteq\cdots$ such that $a_k$ enters the domain of $p_{2k+1}$ (the forth step) and $b_k$ enters the range of $p_{2k+2}$ (the back step), using a property of the structures that lets each finite partial isomorphism grow by one element. The union $\bigcup_kp_k$ is then an isomorphism from $A$ onto $B$.
examples: Cantor's argument shows that any two countable dense [total orders](c:total-order) without endpoints are isomorphic, for example $\mathbb{Q}$ and the dyadic rationals.
The same method shows that any two countable graphs with the extension property are isomorphic, which gives the unique random graph.
Non-example: for $\mathbb{Q}$ and $\mathbb{Z}$ the method fails, because no element of $\mathbb{Z}$ lies between $0$ and $1$ to match $1/2$ (the orders are not isomorphic).

reminder: The bandwidth of a signal is the width of the frequency band outside which its [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) is zero.
definition: For a [band-limited signal](c:band-limited-signal) $f$ whose [Fourier transform](c:fourier-transform) $\hat f$ vanishes outside the positive frequency band $[f_1,f_2]$, the bandwidth is $B=f_2-f_1$ for the smallest such band, measured in hertz. In the Shannon–Hartley theorem the [channel capacity](c:channel-capacity) $C=B\log_2(1+S/N)$ grows with the bandwidth $B$ of the channel.
examples: A voice telephone channel carries the frequencies from $300$ Hz to $3400$ Hz, so its bandwidth is $3100$ Hz.
A baseband audio signal with frequencies between $0$ and $20$ kHz has bandwidth $20$ kHz.
Non-example: a pulse that is nonzero only on a finite time interval is not band-limited, because its nonzero Fourier transform cannot vanish at all large frequencies, so no finite band contains it.

reminder: A base of a structure is a subfamily from which one fixed operation, such as union, recovers the whole structure.
definition: Let $\mathcal S$ be a family of sets that carries a structure, such as the open sets of a topology. A base of $\mathcal S$ is a subfamily $\mathcal B\subseteq\mathcal S$ from which one fixed operation recovers all of $\mathcal S$. For a [topology](c:topology) the operation is union, so every [open set](c:open-set) is a union of members of $\mathcal B$; for a filter it is passing to supersets, and for an ideal it is passing to subsets.
examples: The open intervals $(a,b)$ form a base of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}$, and so do the intervals with rational endpoints.
In a discrete space the singletons $\{x\}$ form a base.
Non-example: the open rays $(a,\infty)$ are open sets but not a base of $\mathbb{R}$, because $(0,1)$ is not a union of rays.

steps: Take the structure to be a [topology](c:topology) $\tau$, the family of open sets of a space.
Let the fixed operation be the union of arbitrary subfamilies.
A base for this structure is a family $\mathcal B\subseteq\tau$ whose unions give every open set.
This is exactly a [base of a topology](c:topological-base).
links.why: It shows that a base of a topology is the case of a base where the generating operation is union.

reminder: Base change along $f:X\to Y$ turns each object over $Y$ into an object over $X$ by pullback.
definition: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a morphism in a [category](c:category) $C$ with [pullbacks](c:pullback). The base change $f^*:C/Y\to C/X$ sends an object $p:E\to Y$ of the [over category](c:over-category) to the projection $E\times_YX\to X$ of the pullback, and it sends a morphism to the induced map of pullbacks. This construction is a [functor](c:functor), because pullbacks are functorial in the object over $Y$.
examples: In sets, $f^*(E\to Y)$ has the fibre $E_{f(x)}$ over each $x\in X$; for the inclusion of one point $y$ it gives the fibre of $E$ over $y$.
In topological spaces, the pullback of a vector bundle $E\to Y$ along a continuous map $f:X\to Y$ is the bundle $f^*E\to X$.
Non-example: composition with $f$, which sends $q:D\to X$ to $f\circ q:D\to Y$, is not base change; it goes from $C/X$ to $C/Y$ and needs no pullbacks.

reminder: For $p\ge2$, each natural number is $\sum a_ip^i$ with digits $0\le a_i<p$ in exactly one way.
definition: Let $p\ge2$ be an [integer](c:integer). The base-$p$ expansion of a [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ is the unique finite string of digits $a_k\dots a_1a_0$ with $0\le a_i<p$ and $n=\sum_{i=0}^ka_ip^i$, where $a_k\ne0$ if $n>0$. The last digit $a_0$ is the remainder of $n$ divided by $p$, and the other digits form the expansion of the quotient.
examples: $13=1\cdot2^3+1\cdot2^2+0\cdot2+1$, so $13$ is written $1101$ in base $2$.
$255=15\cdot16+15$, so $255$ is written $FF$ in base $16$.
Non-example: the string $12$ is not a base-$2$ expansion, because the digit $2$ is not smaller than the base $2$.

steps: Fix the base $p=10$ with the ten digits $0,1,\dots,9$.
Each natural number $n$ then has a unique digit string $a_k\dots a_0$ with $n=\sum a_i10^i$.
This string is the decimal numeral of $n$, so decimal notation is the base-$10$ expansion.
links.why: It shows that decimal notation is the case $p=10$ of the base-$p$ expansion.

reminder: A Beilinson monad is a chain complex with homology in degree $0$ only, so it presents that homology.
definition: A monad in the sense of Beilinson is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $C_\bullet$ whose [homology](c:homology) $H_n(C_\bullet)$ is zero for every $n\ne0$. Such a complex is [quasi-isomorphic](c:quasi-isomorphism) to its one homology object $H_0$ placed in degree $0$, so the monad presents $H_0$ by terms that are easier to describe than $H_0$ itself.
examples: A complex $0\to A\xrightarrow{a}B\xrightarrow{b}C\to0$ with $a$ injective and $b$ surjective, with $B$ placed in degree $0$, has homology $\ker b/\operatorname{im}a$ in degree $0$ only.
A projective resolution of a module $M$ has homology $M$ in degree $0$ and zero homology elsewhere, so it is a monad for $M$.
Non-example: the singular chain complex of the circle has nonzero homology in degrees $0$ and $1$, so it is not a monad.

steps: Start with a Beilinson monad, which is a [chain complex](c:chain-complex) $C_\bullet$.
The added condition is that $H_n(C_\bullet)=0$ for all $n\ne0$.
Then $C_\bullet$ is [quasi-isomorphic](c:quasi-isomorphism) to the single object $H_0(C_\bullet)$ placed in degree $0$.
links.why: It shows that a monad is a chain complex with one extra vanishing condition on its homology.

reminder: A bilinear map is linear in each argument when the other argument stays fixed.
definition: Let $A$, $B$ and $C$ be [vector spaces](c:vector-space), or modules, or abelian groups, with the same scalars. A map $f:A\times B\to C$ on the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) is bilinear when $f(a,-):B\to C$ and $f(-,b):A\to C$ are [linear maps](c:linear-map) for all $a\in A$ and $b\in B$. For abelian groups this says $f(a+a',b)=f(a,b)+f(a',b)$ and $f(a,b+b')=f(a,b)+f(a,b')$.
examples: Multiplication $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$ and the dot product $\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ are bilinear.
Matrix multiplication $M_{m\times n}\times M_{n\times p}\to M_{m\times p}$ and the cross product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ are bilinear.
Non-example: addition $(a,b)\mapsto a+b$ on $\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}$ is not bilinear, because $a+(b+b')\ne(a+b)+(a+b')$ when $a\ne0$.

steps: A [multilinear map](c:multilinear-map) with $n$ arguments is linear in each argument when the others are fixed.
Take $n=2$ with the arguments $a\in A$ and $b\in B$.
The condition becomes linearity in $a$ and linearity in $b$.
So a bilinear map is a multilinear map with two arguments.
links.why: It shows that bilinear maps are the case of two arguments, so facts about multilinear maps apply to them.

steps: Start with a bilinear map $f:V\times W\to C$ of vector spaces over a field $k$.
Choose the target $C=k$, the field of scalars.
Then $f$ is a [bilinear form](c:bilinear-form).
links.why: It shows that a bilinear form is a bilinear map with values in the scalars.

reminder: A binary digit, or bit, is one of the two symbols $0$ and $1$.
definition: A binary digit is an element of the two-element set $\{0,1\}$, also called the [Boolean domain](c:boolean-domain), and it is a digit of base $2$. A [natural number](c:natural-number) is written in binary as a finite string of bits $b_k\dots b_0$ with value $\sum b_i2^i$.
examples: The string $1011$ has four bits, and it stands for $8+2+1=11$.
A byte has eight bits, so it takes $2^8=256$ different values.
Non-example: the symbol $2$ is not a binary digit, because only $0$ and $1$ are.

reminder: A binary operation on a set $S$ takes two elements of $S$ and returns one element of $S$.
definition: A binary operation on a [set](c:set) $S$ is a [function](c:function) $\ast:S\times S\to S$ from the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) $S\times S$ to $S$. It writes $a\ast b$ for the value at $(a,b)$, and this value must lie in $S$ for all $a,b\in S$.
examples: Addition and multiplication on $\mathbb{Z}$ are binary operations, and so is composition of maps on the set of functions $X\to X$.
Union and intersection are binary operations on the [power set](c:power-set) of a set.
Non-example: subtraction is not a binary operation on $\mathbb{N}$, because $2-5\notin\mathbb{N}$.
Non-example: the dot product on $\mathbb{R}^3$ returns a real number and not a vector, so it is not a binary operation on $\mathbb{R}^3$.

steps: Start with a binary operation $\ast$ on a set $S$.
Add the condition $(a\ast b)\ast c=a\ast(b\ast c)$ for all $a,b,c\in S$.
Then $\ast$ is an [associative operation](c:associative-operation).
links.why: It shows that associativity is one extra equation on a binary operation.

reminder: A birational morphism is a morphism that is an isomorphism between dense open subsets of its source and target.
definition: Let $X$ and $Y$ be irreducible [varieties](c:algebraic-variety) over a field. A morphism $f:X\to Y$ is birational when there are [dense](c:dense-set) [open sets](c:open-set) $U\subseteq X$ and $V\subseteq Y$ such that $f$ restricts to an [isomorphism](c:isomorphism) $U\to V$. Equivalently, $f$ induces an isomorphism of [function fields](c:function-field).
examples: The [blow-up](c:blow-up) of $\mathbb{A}^2$ at the origin is a birational morphism to $\mathbb{A}^2$, because it is an isomorphism away from the origin.
The map $t\mapsto(t^2-1,\,t(t^2-1))$ from $\mathbb{A}^1$ onto the nodal curve $y^2=x^2(x+1)$ is birational: it is an isomorphism away from $t=\pm1$.
Non-example: $x\mapsto x^2$ on $\mathbb{A}^1$ is not birational in characteristic different from $2$, because it has degree $2$ and is not injective on any dense open set.

steps: A [birational map](c:birational-map) $X\dashrightarrow Y$ is a rational map that is an isomorphism between dense open subsets.
Take a morphism $f:X\to Y$ with this property.
Then $f$ is a birational map that is defined at every point of $X$.
links.why: It shows that a birational morphism is a birational map with no points of indeterminacy.

steps: Let $f:X\to Y$ be an isomorphism of varieties.
Choose $U=X$ and $V=Y$, which are dense open sets.
Then $f$ restricts to an isomorphism $U\to V$, so $f$ is a birational morphism.
links.why: It shows that every isomorphism is birational, and that a birational morphism is an isomorphism only on dense open sets.

reminder: A BN-pair splits a group $G$ into double cosets $BwB$ that are indexed by a Coxeter group $W$.
definition: A BN-pair in a [group](c:group) $G$ is a pair of [subgroups](c:subgroup) $B,N$ such that $G$ is generated by $B$ and $N$, the intersection $T=B\cap N$ is a [normal subgroup](c:normal-subgroup) of $N$, and the [quotient group](c:quotient-group) $W=N/T$ is generated by a set $S$ of elements of order $2$. Moreover $sBw\subseteq BwB\cup BswB$ for $s\in S$ and $w\in W$, and $sBs\ne B$ for $s\in S$. Then $(W,S)$ is a [Coxeter group](c:coxeter-group) and $G=\bigsqcup_{w\in W}BwB$.
examples: In $GL_n(F)$ take $B$ the upper triangular matrices and $N$ the monomial matrices; then $T$ is the diagonal matrices and $W$ is the symmetric group $S_n$ with the adjacent transpositions as $S$.
In $SL_2(F)$ take $B$ upper triangular and $N$ the monomial matrices of determinant $1$; then $W$ has order $2$ and $SL_2(F)=B\sqcup BsB$.
Non-example: in $G=S_3$ take $B=\{1\}$ and $N=S_3$; they generate $G$ and $T=1$, but $sBs=B$ for every $s$, so the last axiom fails.

reminder: A Boolean formula is satisfiable when some assignment of truth values to its variables makes it true.
definition: A propositional [formula](c:formula) $\varphi$ in the variables $x_1,\dots,x_n$ is satisfiable when some assignment $v:\{x_1,\dots,x_n\}\to\{0,1\}$ of values in the [Boolean domain](c:boolean-domain) makes $\varphi$ evaluate to $1$. A formula that no assignment satisfies is unsatisfiable. Deciding whether a given formula is satisfiable is the SAT problem.
examples: The formula $(x\vee y)\wedge\neg x$ is satisfiable: take $x=0$ and $y=1$.
The formula $(x\vee y)\wedge(\neg x\vee y)\wedge(x\vee\neg y)$ is satisfiable by $x=y=1$.
Non-example: the formula $x\wedge\neg x$ is unsatisfiable, because it is false for both values of $x$.

reminder: A Boolean topos is a [topos](c:topos) in which every [subobject](c:subobject) has a complement.
definition:
A Boolean topos is a [topos](c:topos) $\mathcal E$ in which the [subobjects](c:subobject) of every object form a [Boolean algebra](c:boolean-algebra), so each subobject $A\hookrightarrow X$ has a complement $
eg A$ with $A\vee
eg A=X$ and $A\wedge
eg A=0$. Equivalently, the [subobject classifier](c:classifier) $\Omega$ is the [coproduct](c:coproduct) $1+1$ of the terminal object with itself.
examples: The topos $\mathbf{Set}$ of sets is Boolean, because every subset has a complement.
For every group $G$ the topos of $G$-sets is Boolean, because the complement of a $G$-invariant subset is $G$-invariant.
Non-example: the topos of sheaves on $\mathbb{R}$ is not Boolean, because the open set $(0,\infty)$ has no complement among the open sets.

steps: Every Boolean topos is a [topos](c:topos), so it has finite limits, exponentials and a subobject classifier.
In every topos the subobjects of an object form a Heyting algebra.
The Boolean case adds that $A\vee\neg A=X$ for every subobject $A$ of $X$.
links.why: It shows that a Boolean topos is a topos whose internal logic is classical.

reminder: A Lorentz boost is a hyperbolic rotation that mixes time with one space direction and fixes the other directions.
definition: A Lorentz boost with rapidity $\eta$ along $x$ is the linear map of [Minkowski space](c:minkowski-space) given by $t'=t\cosh\eta+x\sinh\eta$ and $x'=x\cosh\eta+t\sinh\eta$ in units with $c=1$, which fixes the other coordinates. It is an element of the [Lorentz group](c:lorentz-group) that lies outside the rotation subgroup $SO(d-1)$ of the [special orthogonal group](c:special-orthogonal-group), and its velocity is $v=\tanh\eta$.
examples: The boost with velocity $v$ along $x$ is $t'=\gamma(t+vx)$ and $x'=\gamma(x+vt)$ with $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-v^2}$.
In one space dimension the boosts form a group isomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$, because rapidities add: composing boosts with $\eta_1$ and $\eta_2$ gives the boost with $\eta_1+\eta_2$.
Non-example: a rotation of the space coordinates $(x,y)$ preserves the Minkowski form but does not mix time with space, so it is not a boost.

reminder: A bottom element of a poset lies below every element of the poset.
definition: In a [poset](c:partial-order) $P$, a bottom is an element $\bot\in P$ with $\bot\le a$ for every $a\in P$. A bottom is unique if it exists: two bottoms $\bot$ and $\bot'$ satisfy $\bot\le\bot'\le\bot$, so they are equal.
examples: The number $0$ is the bottom of $(\mathbb{N},\le)$, and $\varnothing$ is the bottom of the [power set](c:power-set) of any set ordered by inclusion.
In the divisibility order on the positive integers, $1$ is the bottom.
Non-example: $(\mathbb{Z},\le)$ has no bottom, because $-n-1<-n$ for every $n$.
Non-example: the nonempty subsets of $\{1,2\}$ ordered by inclusion have no bottom, because $\{1\}$ and $\{2\}$ are minimal and neither lies below the other.

steps: View the poset $P$ as a [category](c:category) with one arrow $a\to b$ exactly when $a\le b$.
A bottom $\bot$ has $\bot\le a$ for all $a$, so there is an arrow $\bot\to a$ for every $a$.
There is at most one arrow between two objects, so this arrow is unique.
So $\bot$ is an [initial object](c:initial-object) of the category $P$.
links.why: It shows that a bottom is an initial object, so facts about initial objects apply to bottoms.

reminder: A function on $[a,b]$ has bounded variation when the sums $\sum|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|$ over all partitions have a finite supremum.
definition: For a function $f$ on a [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[a,b]$, the total variation is $V_a^b(f)=\sup\sum_{i=1}^n|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|$, where the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) runs over all partitions $a=x_0<x_1<\dots<x_n=b$. The function $f$ has bounded variation when $V_a^b(f)<\infty$. By Jordan's theorem, these are exactly the differences of two [monotone functions](c:monotone-function).
examples: Every monotone function on $[a,b]$ has bounded variation, with $V_a^b(f)=|f(b)-f(a)|$.
Every [Lipschitz continuous function](c:lipschitz-continuous-function) with constant $L$ has $V_a^b(f)\le L(b-a)$.
Non-example: $f(x)=x\sin(1/x)$ with $f(0)=0$ is continuous on $[0,1]$ but does not have bounded variation, because $V_0^1(f)=\infty$.

steps: Let $f$ be increasing on $[a,b]$.
For every partition the sum $\sum|f(x_i)-f(x_{i-1})|$ telescopes to $f(b)-f(a)$.
So $V_a^b(f)=f(b)-f(a)<\infty$ and $f$ has bounded variation.
The general case also allows a difference of two increasing functions, so $f$ may go up and down.
links.why: It shows that bounded variation extends monotonicity to functions that are differences of monotone functions.

steps: Let $f$ be [absolutely continuous](c:absolutely-continuous-function) on $[a,b]$ and take $\varepsilon=1$ in its definition, which gives some $\delta>0$.
Split $[a,b]$ into $N$ pieces of length less than $\delta$.
On each piece the sum over any partition is at most $1$, because its intervals are disjoint with total length less than $\delta$.
So $V_a^b(f)\le N$, and $f$ has bounded variation.
links.why: It shows that absolutely continuous functions have bounded variation, so results for bounded variation apply to them.

reminder: For a spectrum $E$, the localization $L_E$ inverts exactly the maps that become equivalences after smashing with $E$.
definition: Let $E$ be a spectrum. A map $f:X\to Y$ of spectra is an $E$-equivalence when $E\wedge f$, the [smash product](c:smash-product-of-spectra) with $E$, is an equivalence, and a spectrum $Z$ is $E$-local when every map $A\to Z$ from a spectrum $A$ with $E\wedge A\simeq0$ is null. The Bousfield localization $L_E$ sends a spectrum $X$ to an $E$-local spectrum $L_EX$ with an $E$-equivalence $X\to L_EX$; it is the [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization) of the [stable homotopy category](c:stable-homotopy-category) at the $E$-equivalences.
examples: For $E=H\mathbb{Q}$ the localization is rationalization, $L_EX=X\wedge H\mathbb{Q}$, and $L_E$ of the sphere spectrum is $H\mathbb{Q}$.
For $E$ the [sphere spectrum](c:sphere-spectrum), the $E$-equivalences are the equivalences, so every spectrum is $E$-local and $L_E$ is the identity.
Non-example: the sphere spectrum is not $H\mathbb{Q}$-local, because $S\to H\mathbb{Q}$ is not an equivalence ($\pi_0S=\mathbb{Z}$ but $\pi_0H\mathbb{Q}=\mathbb{Q}$).

steps: A [Bousfield localization](c:bousfield-localization) inverts a chosen class $W$ of maps in a homotopy theory.
Take the homotopy theory to be the stable homotopy category of spectra.
Take $W$ to be the $E$-equivalences, the maps that become equivalences after smashing with $E$.
The resulting localization is $L_E$.
links.why: It shows that $L_E$ is an ordinary Bousfield localization with one particular class of maps inverted.

reminder: A box in $\mathbb{R}^\iota$ is a product of half-open intervals $(l_i,u_i]$ with $l_i<u_i$ in every coordinate.
definition: Let $\iota$ be a finite index set and let $l,u:\iota\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $l_i<u_i$ for all $i$. The box with corners $l$ and $u$ is the set $\{x\in\mathbb{R}^\iota: l_i<x_i\le u_i\text{ for all }i\}$, the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) of the half-open [intervals](c:interval) $(l_i,u_i]$ of [real numbers](c:real-number). The condition $l_i<u_i$ makes every side of the box nonempty.
examples: For $\iota=\{1,2\}$, the box with $l=(0,0)$ and $u=(1,2)$ is the rectangle $(0,1]\times(0,2]$ in the plane.
For one coordinate, a box is a half-open interval $(a,b]$ with $a<b$.
Non-example: the closed square $[0,1]^2$ is not a box, because a box is half-open and leaves out its lower faces.
Non-example: the segment $(0,1]\times\{0\}$ is not a box, because $l_2=u_2$ for the second coordinate.

reminder: The braid group $B_n$ is the group of braids on $n$ strands under stacking, with generators $\sigma_i$ that swap adjacent strands.
definition: The braid group $B_n$ is the [group](c:group) with generators $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$ and relations $\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i=\sigma_{i+1}\sigma_i\sigma_{i+1}$ and $\sigma_i\sigma_j=\sigma_j\sigma_i$ for $|i-j|\ge2$, so it is a [finitely presented group](c:finitely-presented-group). Equivalently, it is the [fundamental group](c:fundamental-group) of the [configuration space](c:configuration-space-of-points) of $n$ unordered points in the plane, whose loops are motions of $n$ points that return to the starting set. Sending $\sigma_i$ to the transposition $(i\ i{+}1)$ gives a surjection onto the [symmetric group](c:symmetric-group).
examples: $B_1$ is trivial and $B_2\cong\mathbb{Z}$, generated by $\sigma_1$.
$B_3$ is generated by $\sigma_1,\sigma_2$ with $\sigma_1\sigma_2\sigma_1=\sigma_2\sigma_1\sigma_2$, and it is infinite and not abelian.
Non-example: the symmetric group $S_n$ is not $B_n$, because $\sigma_i^2=1$ in $S_n$ but $\sigma_i$ has infinite order in $B_n$.

steps: The group $B_n$ has the finite generating set $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_{n-1}$.
Its defining relations are the finite list of braid relations.
A group with finitely many generators and finitely many relations is a [finitely presented group](c:finitely-presented-group).
links.why: It shows that every braid group has a finite presentation that can be used in computations.

reminder: A branched cover is a map that is a covering map away from a small closed set of branch points.
definition: A continuous map $p:X\to Y$ of [topological spaces](c:topological-space) is a branched cover when there is a closed, nowhere dense set $B\subseteq Y$, the branch locus, such that $p$ restricts to a [covering space](c:covering-space) map $X\setminus p^{-1}(B)\to Y\setminus B$. Over a point of $B$ several sheets may merge, so the fibre can have fewer points than over nearby points. Usually one also asks that $p$ is finite-to-one and that $p^{-1}(B)$ is nowhere dense in $X$.
examples: The map $z\mapsto z^2$ from $\mathbb{C}$ to $\mathbb{C}$ is a branched cover with $B=\{0\}$: it is a two-sheeted covering over $\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$, and the sheets merge at $0$.
The projection $(x,y)\mapsto x$ of the curve $y^2=x(x-1)(x+1)$ onto the $x$-line is a double branched cover, branched over $0$, $1$, $-1$ and $\infty$.
Non-example: the constant map $S^1\to\{\ast\}$ is not a branched cover, because its branch locus would be the whole base, which is not nowhere dense.

steps: Let $p:X\to Y$ be a [covering space](c:covering-space) map.
Choose the branch locus $B=\varnothing$, which is closed and nowhere dense.
Then $p$ is a covering map outside $B$, so $p$ is a branched cover with no branch points.
links.why: It shows that a branched cover is a covering that is allowed to fail over a small closed set.

reminder: A branched covering of Riemann surfaces is a non-constant holomorphic map that is a covering map except over finitely many points.
definition: Let $X$ and $Y$ be compact connected [Riemann surfaces](c:riemann-surface). A branched covering is a non-constant [holomorphic map](c:holomorphic-function) $f:X\to Y$ such that, for some finite set $B\subset Y$ of branch values, $f$ is a finite-sheeted [covering space](c:covering-space) map over $Y\setminus B$. Near every point of $X$, $f$ looks like $z\mapsto z^e$ in suitable local coordinates, where $e\ge1$ is the ramification index.
examples: Every non-constant rational function $\mathbb{P}^1\to\mathbb{P}^1$ is a branched covering, for example $z\mapsto z^3$ with branch values $0$ and $\infty$.
The map $f(z)=z^2(3-2z)$ on the [Riemann sphere](c:riemann-sphere) has degree $3$ and is branched only over $0$, $1$ and $\infty$.
Non-example: $\exp:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0\}$ is not a branched covering in this sense, because its source is not compact and it has infinitely many sheets.

steps: Let $f:X\to Y$ be a branched covering of compact Riemann surfaces, with a finite branch set $B$.
A finite set in $Y$ is closed and nowhere dense, because $Y$ has no isolated points.
Over $Y\setminus B$ the map $f$ is a covering map, by the definition.
So $f$ is a [branched cover](c:branched-cover) in the topological sense, with extra holomorphic structure.
links.why: It shows that a branched covering of Riemann surfaces is a branched cover with a finite branch set and a holomorphic map.

reminder: Breadth-first search visits the vertices of a graph in layers: first the start, then its neighbours, then their new neighbours.
definition: Breadth-first search from a start vertex $s$ of a [graph](c:graph) keeps a first-in first-out queue: it takes the front vertex, marks each unseen neighbour as visited, and adds it to the back of the queue. It visits all vertices at distance $k$ from $s$ before any vertex at distance $k+1$, so in a [connected graph](c:connected-graph) it reaches every vertex and gives the shortest-path distances from $s$. The edges that first reach each vertex form a spanning [tree](c:tree).
examples: In the path $a-b-c-d$ started at $b$, the visiting order is $b$, then $a$ and $c$, then $d$.
In an unweighted graph, breadth-first search gives the fewest steps between two vertices, such as the fewest moves of a knight between two squares of a chessboard.
Non-example: depth-first search also visits every vertex of a connected graph, but it follows one path as far as it can before it returns, so it does not give shortest distances.

reminder: The Burnside ring of a finite group $G$ is the ring of finite $G$-sets, with disjoint union as sum and Cartesian product as product.
definition: Let $G$ be a [finite group](c:finite-group). The Burnside ring $A(G)$ is the Grothendieck group of the commutative monoid of isomorphism classes of finite [G-sets](c:group-action) under [disjoint union](c:disjoint-union), with multiplication given by the [Cartesian product](c:cartesian-product) with the diagonal action. As an abelian group it is free with basis the classes $[G/H]$, where $H$ runs over the conjugacy classes of subgroups of $G$.
examples: For the trivial group, $A(G)=\mathbb{Z}$, because a finite set is determined by its size.
For $G=C_2$ the ring $A(G)$ has basis $1=[C_2/C_2]$ and $x=[C_2/1]$ with $x^2=2x$, so $A(C_2)\cong\mathbb{Z}[x]/(x^2-2x)$.
Non-example: the monoid of isomorphism classes of finite $G$-sets is not the Burnside ring, because it has no negatives; the ring adds formal differences.

reminder: $C[0,1]$ is the Banach space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ with the supremum norm.
definition: $C[0,1]$ is the set of [continuous functions](c:continuous-function) $f:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$) on the [closed interval](c:closed-interval) $[0,1]$, with the [norm](c:norm) $\|f\|=\sup_{x\in[0,1]}|f(x)|$. With this norm it is a [Banach space](c:banach-space), because a uniform limit of continuous functions is continuous.
examples: The polynomials lie in $C[0,1]$ and are [dense](c:dense-set) there, by the Weierstrass approximation theorem.
The function $f(x)=x^2$ has $\|f\|=1$, and so has $g(x)=\sin(\pi x)$.
Non-example: the step function equal to $0$ on $[0,1/2)$ and to $1$ on $[1/2,1]$ is not in $C[0,1]$, because it jumps at $1/2$.
Non-example: the continuous functions with the integral norm $\int_0^1|f|$ are not complete, so that normed space is not $C[0,1]$.

steps: Take the space $K=[0,1]$.
The closed interval $[0,1]$ is a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space).
So the space $C(K)$ of continuous functions on $K$ with the supremum norm is defined.
For $K=[0,1]$ this space is $C[0,1]$.
links.why: It shows that every result for $C(K)$ spaces holds for $C[0,1]$.

reminder: The Whitney $C^\infty$ topology makes two smooth maps close when all their derivatives are close at every point of the domain.
definition: Let $X$ and $Y$ be [smooth manifolds](c:smooth-manifold), and let $j^kf:X\to J^k(X,Y)$ be the $k$-th order prolongation of a [smooth function](c:smooth-function) $f$ into the [jet bundle](c:jet-bundle). The Whitney $C^\infty$ topology on $C^\infty(X,Y)$ is the [topology](c:topology) generated by the sets $\{f:j^kf(X)\subseteq U\}$ for all $k\ge0$ and all open sets $U\subseteq J^k(X,Y)$. A neighbourhood of $f$ thus bounds the difference between $f$ and its derivatives of each finite order by a positive function on $X$, which may shrink toward infinity.
examples: For compact $X$, a sequence $f_n$ converges to $f$ in this topology exactly when all derivatives of $f_n$ converge uniformly to those of $f$.
For $X=Y=\mathbb{R}$, the sets $\{f:|f^{(i)}(x)|<\varepsilon(x)\text{ for }i\le k\}$ with $\varepsilon$ a positive continuous function form a neighbourhood base of $0$.
Non-example: the compact-open topology is not the Whitney $C^\infty$ topology, because $f_n(x)=x/n$ tends to $0$ uniformly on compact sets but not in the Whitney topology.

reminder: For a compact Hausdorff space $K$, $C(K)$ is the Banach space of continuous scalar functions on $K$ with the supremum norm.
definition: Let $K$ be a [compact Hausdorff space](c:compact-hausdorff-space). $C(K)$ is the set of [continuous functions](c:continuous-function) $K\to\mathbb{R}$ (or $\mathbb{C}$) with the norm $\|f\|=\max_{x\in K}|f(x)|$, and it is a [Banach space](c:banach-space). By the Banach–Stone theorem, if $C(K)$ and $C(L)$ are isometric as Banach spaces, then $K$ and $L$ are [homeomorphic](c:homeomorphism).
examples: If $K=\{1,\dots,n\}$ has the discrete topology, then $C(K)$ is $\mathbb{R}^n$ with the maximum norm.
If $K$ is a compact metric space, then $C(K)$ is a separable Banach space; the case $K=[0,1]$ is $C[0,1]$.
Non-example: for $K=(0,1)$, which is not compact, the continuous function $1/x$ has infinite supremum norm, so the continuous functions on $K$ do not form a $C(K)$ space.

steps: Take the compact Hausdorff space $K=[0,1]$.
Then $C(K)$ is the space of continuous functions on $[0,1]$ with the supremum norm.
That space is $C[0,1]$.
links.why: It shows that $C[0,1]$ is the best-known case of a $C(K)$ space.

reminder: A $C_0$-semigroup is a family $T(t)$ of bounded operators with $T(0)=I$, $T(s+t)=T(s)T(t)$ and $T(t)x\to x$ as $t\to0^+$.
definition: A $C_0$-semigroup on a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$ is a family $(T(t))_{t\ge0}$ of [bounded linear operators](c:bounded-linear-operator) with $T(0)=I$ and $T(s+t)=T(s)T(t)$ for all $s,t\ge0$, which is continuous at $0$ in the [strong operator topology](c:strong-operator-topology): $\|T(t)x-x\|\to0$ as $t\to0^+$ for each $x\in X$. Then $t\mapsto T(t)x$ is continuous on $[0,\infty)$ for every $x$, and the generator $Ax=\lim_{t\to0^+}(T(t)x-x)/t$ is a closed, densely defined operator.
examples: On $L^p(\mathbb{R})$ with $1\le p<\infty$ the translation semigroup $(T(t)f)(x)=f(x+t)$ is a $C_0$-semigroup.
For a bounded operator $A$ the exponential $T(t)=e^{tA}=\sum_{n\ge0}t^nA^n/n!$ is a $C_0$-semigroup.
The heat semigroup $e^{t\Delta}$ on $L^2(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a $C_0$-semigroup.
Non-example: translation on $L^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ is a semigroup but not strongly continuous, because for $f=1_{[0,1]}$ we get $\|T(t)f-f\|_\infty=1$ for every $t>0$.

steps: Let $(T(t))_{t\ge0}$ be a $C_0$-semigroup on $X$.
Its operators satisfy $T(s)T(t)=T(s+t)$, so the set of all $T(t)$ is closed under composition.
Composition of operators is associative, so this set is a [semigroup](c:semigroup), and it is a monoid with unit $T(0)=I$.
The $C_0$ case adds that $T(t)x\to x$ as $t\to0^+$ for every $x$.
links.why: It shows that a $C_0$-semigroup is an operator semigroup with one continuity condition at $0$.

reminder: A Calabi-Yau manifold is a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) whose [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle) is trivial.
definition: A Calabi-Yau manifold of dimension $n$ is a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) $M$ whose [canonical bundle](c:canonical-bundle) $K_M=\Lambda^nT^*M$ is trivial, so $c_1(M)=0$. By Yau's theorem, such an $M$ has a Kähler metric with zero [Ricci curvature](c:ricci-curvature) in every Kähler class. Some authors also require $H^i(M,\mathcal O_M)=0$ for $0<i<n$.
examples: An [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) $\mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ is a Calabi-Yau manifold of dimension $1$, because $dz$ trivializes its canonical bundle.
A smooth quartic surface in $\mathbb{P}^3$ (a K3 surface) and a smooth quintic threefold in $\mathbb{P}^4$ are Calabi-Yau manifolds of dimension $2$ and $3$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{P}^n$ is compact and Kähler but not Calabi-Yau, because its canonical bundle $\mathcal O(-n-1)$ is not trivial.
Non-example: a compact Riemann surface of genus $g\ge2$ is not Calabi-Yau, because its canonical bundle has degree $2g-2>0$.

steps: A Calabi-Yau manifold $M$ is a compact [Kähler manifold](c:kahler-manifold) by definition.
The extra condition is that the canonical bundle $K_M$ is trivial.
This forces $c_1(M)=0$, and Yau's theorem then gives a Ricci-flat Kähler metric.
links.why: It shows that a Calabi-Yau manifold is a compact Kähler manifold with one extra condition on the canonical bundle.

reminder: A canonical transformation is a change of phase-space coordinates that preserves the symplectic form and the form of Hamilton's equations.
definition: A canonical transformation is a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) $\varphi:M\to M'$ between [symplectic manifolds](c:symplectic-manifold), the phase spaces, with $\varphi^*\omega'=\omega$ for their [symplectic forms](c:symplectic-form). In canonical coordinates $(q,p)\mapsto(Q,P)$ this says $\{Q_i,Q_j\}=0$, $\{P_i,P_j\}=0$ and $\{Q_i,P_j\}=\delta_{ij}$ for the [Poisson bracket](c:poisson-bracket).
examples: Translations $(q,p)\mapsto(q+a,p+b)$ and the rotation $(q,p)\mapsto(p,-q)$ are canonical transformations.
The time-$t$ flow map of any Hamiltonian system is a canonical transformation.
Non-example: $(q,p)\mapsto(2q,p)$ is not canonical, because it multiplies $dq\wedge dp$ by $2$.

steps: A canonical transformation is a [diffeomorphism](c:diffeomorph) of phase space.
The added condition is that it preserves the symplectic form, $\varphi^*\omega'=\omega$.
So the canonical transformations form a subclass of the diffeomorphisms of phase space.
links.why: It shows that a canonical transformation is a diffeomorphism with one extra condition, preservation of the symplectic form.

steps: Let $\varphi$ be a [Hamiltonian diffeomorphism](c:hamiltonian-diffeomorphism), the time-one flow of a time-dependent Hamiltonian $H$.
Along the flow, $\mathcal L_{X_H}\omega=d\,\iota_{X_H}\omega=\pm\,d(dH)=0$, so $\omega$ stays constant.
So $\varphi^*\omega=\omega$, and $\varphi$ is a canonical transformation.
The converse fails in general, for example for some translations of the torus $T^2$.
links.why: It shows that every Hamiltonian flow is canonical, and that canonical transformations are the larger class.

reminder: The cap product sends a degree $p$ cohomology class and a degree $n$ homology class to a class in $H_{n-p}$.
definition: For a [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ and a coefficient ring $R$, the cap product is the pairing $\cap:H_n(X;R)\otimes H^p(X;R)\to H_{n-p}(X;R)$ of [singular](c:singular-cohomology) [homology](c:ordinary-homology) and [cohomology](c:ordinary-cohomology). On chains it is given by $\sigma\cap\varphi=\varphi(\sigma|_{[v_0,\dots,v_p]})\,\sigma|_{[v_p,\dots,v_n]}$ for a singular $n$-simplex $\sigma$ and a $p$-cochain $\varphi$, and it descends to classes because $\partial(\sigma\cap\varphi)=\pm(\partial\sigma\cap\varphi-\sigma\cap\delta\varphi)$.
examples: For a closed oriented $n$-manifold $M$ with [fundamental class](c:fundamental-class) $[M]$, the map $\varphi\mapsto[M]\cap\varphi$ from $H^p(M)$ to $H_{n-p}(M)$ is an isomorphism, which is Poincaré duality.
For $p=0$ we get $\sigma\cap\varphi=\varphi(v_0)\,\sigma$, so the cap product with the $0$-cochain $1$ is the identity.
Non-example: the [cup product](c:cup-product) $H^p\times H^q\to H^{p+q}$ pairs two cohomology classes and gives a cohomology class, so it is not the cap product.

steps: Take a class $\varphi\in H^n(X;R)$ and a class $[\sigma]\in H_n(X;R)$ of the same degree $n$.
Their cap product $[\sigma]\cap\varphi$ lies in $H_0(X;R)$.
The augmentation $H_0(X;R)\to R$ adds up the coefficients of a $0$-chain.
Applied to $[\sigma]\cap\varphi$ it gives the number $\varphi(\sigma)$, which is the [Kronecker pairing](c:kronecker-pairing).
links.why: It shows that the Kronecker pairing is the cap product in equal degrees followed by the augmentation.

reminder: A positive measure $\mu$ on the unit disc is Carleson when $\mu(S(I))\le C|I|$ for every boundary arc $I$.
definition: Let $\mathbb{D}$ be the [unit disc](c:unit-disc). For an arc $I$ of the unit circle, with length $|I|$ normalized so that the circle has length $1$, let $S(I)=\{re^{i\theta}:e^{i\theta}\in I,\ 1-|I|\le r<1\}$ be the Carleson box over $I$. A positive [Borel measure](c:borel-measure) $\mu$ on $\mathbb{D}$ is a Carleson measure when $\mu(S(I))\le C|I|$ for some constant $C$ and every arc $I$; equivalently, $\int|f|^2d\mu\le C'\|f\|^2_{H^2}$ for every $f$ in the [Hardy space](c:hardy-space) $H^2$.
examples: The area measure $dA$ on $\mathbb{D}$ is a Carleson measure, because $A(S(I))$ is about $|I|^2\le C|I|$.
For an interpolating sequence $(z_n)$ in $\mathbb{D}$, the measure $\sum_n(1-|z_n|)\,\delta_{z_n}$, made of [Dirac measures](c:dirac-measure), is a Carleson measure (Carleson's theorem).
Non-example: the sum of unit masses at $z_n=1-2^{-n}$ is not a Carleson measure, because the box over an arc of length $2^{-k}$ centred at $1$ contains infinitely many points.

reminder: A Carmichael number is a composite number $n$ with $a^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n$ for every $a$ that is coprime to $n$.
definition: A Carmichael number is a composite [natural number](c:natural-number) $n$ such that $a^{n-1}\equiv1\pmod n$ for every integer $a$ [coprime](c:coprime-integers) to $n$. By Korselt's criterion, a composite $n$ is a Carmichael number exactly when $n$ is [squarefree](c:squarefree-integer) and $p-1$ divides $n-1$ for every [prime](c:prime-number) $p$ that divides $n$.
examples: $561=3\cdot11\cdot17$ is the smallest Carmichael number, because $2$, $10$ and $16$ divide $560$.
$1105=5\cdot13\cdot17$ and $1729=7\cdot13\cdot19$ are Carmichael numbers.
Non-example: $15$ is composite but $2^{14}\equiv4\pmod{15}$, so $15$ is not a Carmichael number.
Non-example: a prime $p$ satisfies the congruence for every $a$ coprime to $p$, but it is excluded because it is not composite.

reminder: When a column sum reaches the base $b$, carrying writes the sum minus $b$ and adds $1$ to the next column.
definition: Write two [natural numbers](c:natural-number) in a base $b$, as in a [base expansion](c:base-p-expansion), and add them column by column from the right. When the sum $s$ of the two digits and the incoming carry satisfies $s\ge b$, the column gets the digit $s-b$ and sends the carry $1$ to the next column. This is correct because $s\cdot b^i=(s-b)\,b^i+1\cdot b^{i+1}$.
examples: In base $10$, the column sum $7+5=12$ gives the digit $2$ and the carry $1$.
In base $2$, $1+1$ gives the digit $0$ and the carry $1$, so $11_2+1_2=100_2$.
Non-example: in $123+456$ no column sum reaches $10$, so no carry happens.

reminder: The Cartan calculus is the set of relations among $d$, $\iota_X$ and $\mathcal L_X$ on differential forms, such as $\mathcal L_X=d\iota_X+\iota_Xd$.
definition: On the [differential forms](c:differential-form) of a manifold, the Cartan calculus consists of the [exterior derivative](c:exterior-derivative) $d$, the [interior product](c:interior-product) $\iota_X$ and the [Lie derivative](c:lie-derivative) $\mathcal L_X$ for each [vector field](c:vector-field) $X$. They satisfy $\mathcal L_X=[d,\iota_X]=d\iota_X+\iota_Xd$, $d^2=0$, $[\mathcal L_X,d]=0$, $[\iota_X,\iota_Y]=0$, $[\mathcal L_X,\iota_Y]=\iota_{[X,Y]}$ and $[\mathcal L_X,\mathcal L_Y]=\mathcal L_{[X,Y]}$, where the brackets with operators are graded commutators.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}$ with $X=\partial_x$ and $\omega=f\,dx$ we get $\mathcal L_X\omega=f'\,dx$, and $d\iota_X\omega=df=f'\,dx$ while $\iota_Xd\omega=0$.
For a closed form $\omega$ the formula gives $\mathcal L_X\omega=d(\iota_X\omega)$, which is exact.
Non-example: the equation $\mathcal L_X=d\iota_X$ alone is false, because for $\omega=x\,dy$ and $X=\partial_x$ we get $\iota_X\omega=0$ but $\mathcal L_X\omega=dy$.

reminder: A Cartesian fibration is an inner fibration where each edge into $p(x)$ lifts to a Cartesian edge into $x$.
definition: A map $p:X\to Y$ of [simplicial sets](c:simplicial-set) is a Cartesian fibration when it is an [inner fibration](c:inner-fibration) and, for every vertex $x$ of $X$ and every edge $f:y\to p(x)$ of $Y$, there is a $p$-[Cartesian](c:cartesian-morphism) edge $e:x'\to x$ of $X$ with $p(e)=f$. For [quasi-categories](c:quasi-category) $X$ and $Y$, this means that the fibres of $p$ depend contravariantly on points of $Y$, and the straightening of $p$ is a functor $Y^{op}\to\mathrm{Cat}_\infty$.
examples: For a category $\mathcal C$ with pullbacks, the target map $\mathrm{Fun}(\Delta^1,\mathcal C)\to\mathcal C$ is a Cartesian fibration, and its Cartesian edges are the pullback squares.
The nerve of a [Grothendieck fibration](c:grothendieck-fibration) of ordinary categories is a Cartesian fibration.

Non-example: the map from the discrete two-point category $\{x_0,x_1\}$ to $[1]=(0\to1)$ with $x_i\mapsto i$ is an inner fibration but not Cartesian, because the edge $0\to1$ has no lift ending at $x_1$.

steps: Let $p:X\to Y$ be a Cartesian fibration of simplicial sets.
By definition $p$ is an [inner fibration](c:inner-fibration), so it has fillers for inner horns.
The Cartesian case adds that every edge $y\to p(x)$ has a Cartesian lift ending at $x$.
links.why: It shows that a Cartesian fibration is an inner fibration with an extra lifting property for edges.

steps: Let $p:E\to B$ be a [Grothendieck fibration](c:grothendieck-fibration) of ordinary categories.
The nerve $N(p)$ is an inner fibration, because nerves of categories have unique fillers for inner horns.
A Cartesian morphism of $p$ gives a Cartesian edge of $N(p)$.
Every morphism of $B$ has a Cartesian lift, so $N(p)$ is a Cartesian fibration.
links.why: It shows that Cartesian fibrations of quasi-categories extend Grothendieck fibrations of ordinary categories.

reminder: A morphism $\hat f$ is $p$-Cartesian when maps into its target that factor through $p(\hat f)$ factor uniquely through $\hat f$.
definition: Let $p:X\to Y$ be a [functor](c:functor) of [categories](c:category). A morphism $\hat f:x\to x'$ of $X$ is $p$-Cartesian when, for every morphism $g:z\to x'$ and every $h:p(z)\to p(x)$ with $p(\hat f)\circ h=p(g)$, there is a unique $g':z\to x$ with $p(g')=h$ and $\hat f\circ g'=g$. This is a [universal property](c:universal-property): $\hat f$ is the universal lift of $p(\hat f)$ with target $x'$.
examples: For $p=\mathrm{cod}:\mathrm{Arr}(\mathcal C)\to\mathcal C$, a morphism of arrows is $p$-Cartesian exactly when its commutative square is a [pullback](c:pullback) square.
For the functor from vector bundles to base spaces, a bundle map is Cartesian when it is an isomorphism on each [fibre](c:fiber).

Non-example: in $\mathrm{Arr}(\mathbf{Set})\to\mathbf{Set}$ the square from $\varnothing\to1$ to $1\to1$ over $\mathrm{id}_1$ is not Cartesian, because the pullback of $1\to1$ along $\mathrm{id}_1$ is $1$ and not $\varnothing$.

steps: Let $\hat f:x\to x'$ be an isomorphism in $X$, and let $g:z\to x'$ and $h$ satisfy $p(\hat f)\circ h=p(g)$.
Put $g'=\hat f^{-1}\circ g$; then $\hat f\circ g'=g$ and $p(g')=p(\hat f)^{-1}p(g)=h$.
If $g''$ is another lift, then $g''=\hat f^{-1}\hat f g''=\hat f^{-1}g=g'$.
So $\hat f$ is $p$-Cartesian, and every isomorphism is Cartesian for every functor $p$.
links.why: It shows that isomorphisms are Cartesian for every functor, so Cartesian morphisms generalize isomorphisms.

reminder: A Casimir element is an element of the center of the universal enveloping algebra $U(\mathfrak g)$.
definition: For a [Lie algebra](c:lie-algebra) $\mathfrak g$, a Casimir element is an element of the [center](c:center) of the [universal enveloping algebra](c:universal-enveloping-algebra) $U(\mathfrak g)$. If $\mathfrak g$ is semisimple with a nondegenerate invariant form and dual bases $(x_i)$ and $(x^i)$, then $C=\sum_ix_ix^i$ is such an element. In every [representation](c:lie-algebra-representation) $C$ acts by an operator that commutes with all of $\mathfrak g$, and by a scalar on each irreducible finite-dimensional representation over an algebraically closed field.
examples: In $U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ with $[e,f]=h$ and $[h,e]=2e$, the element $C=ef+fe+\tfrac12h^2$ is central, and it acts as $n(n+2)/2$ on the irreducible representation of highest weight $n$.
For $\mathfrak{so}(3)$ with angular momentum operators $L_x,L_y,L_z$, the element $L^2=L_x^2+L_y^2+L_z^2$ is a Casimir element.
Non-example: $h\in U(\mathfrak{sl}_2)$ is not central, because $he-eh=2e\ne0$.

reminder: A Casson handle is an infinite tower of kinky handles that replaces a $2$-handle in a $4$-manifold.
definition: A kinky handle is a thickened [immersed](c:immersion) [disc](c:ball) with finitely many double points in a $4$-[manifold](c:manifold), attached along a neighbourhood of its boundary circle. A Casson handle is built in infinitely many stages: stage one is a kinky handle, and at each later stage a new kinky handle is attached along a circle that belongs to each double point of the previous stage. The Casson handle is the union of all stages, without the attaching regions of the handles still to come.
examples: A Casson handle is described by a rooted tree with signs: each vertex is a kinky handle and each edge is a double point with its sign.
Freedman proved that every Casson handle is homeomorphic to the open $2$-handle $D^2\times\mathbb{R}^2$ with attaching region $\partial D^2\times\mathbb{R}^2$.
Non-example: a kinky handle with only finitely many stages is not a Casson handle, because a new kinky handle must be attached at every double point at every stage.

reminder: Cat is the 2-category whose objects are small categories, whose morphisms are functors and whose 2-morphisms are natural transformations.
definition: Cat has the [small categories](c:small-category) as objects, the [functors](c:functor) between them as morphisms, and the [natural transformations](c:natural-transformation) between functors as 2-morphisms. Composition of functors, together with vertical and horizontal composition of natural transformations, makes it a strict [2-category](c:2-category). Only small categories are allowed, so Cat is a large category and is not an object of itself.
examples: The terminal category $\mathbf1$ and the arrow category $[1]=(0\to1)$ are objects of Cat, and a functor $\mathbf1\to\mathcal C$ picks an object of $\mathcal C$.
Every group $G$ gives a one-object category $BG$, and a functor $BG\to BH$ is a group homomorphism.
Non-example: Cat is not the category of all categories, because it leaves out large categories such as $\mathbf{Set}$, and it is not an object of itself.

steps: A [2-category](c:2-category) has objects, morphisms between objects and 2-morphisms between morphisms.
In Cat the objects are small categories, the morphisms are functors and the 2-morphisms are natural transformations.
Composition of functors and the two compositions of natural transformations satisfy the 2-category axioms.
So Cat is a strict 2-category.
links.why: It shows that Cat is the model example of a 2-category, so 2-categorical facts apply to categories, functors and natural transformations.
